newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladeshis welcome trial, divided on impact.
newsitem.headline: Bangladeshis welcome trial, divided on impact.

text.p: The long-awaited trial that opened in Bangladesh this week over the assassination of independence leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman in 1975 has won broad support as a belated, but welcome, affirmation of the rule of law.

But some analysts worry that the trial could open old wounds and destroy attempts to establish the political stability that this young and impoverished nation desperately needs under its present prime minister, Sheikh Mujib's daughter Sheikh Hasina.

In all 32 people, including Mujib, his wife and three sons were killed in August 1975 in Bangladesh's first army revolt. Sheikh Hasina and her sister, Sheikh Rehana, survived as they were travelling abroad at the time of the coup.

A total of 25 people have been implicated in Mujib's assassination and six of the accused, including three ex-army officers and Mujib's information minister Taheruddin Thakur, appeared in court on Monday, when a formal hearing of the charges was set for February 20.

The trial was made possible when the Bangladesh parliament, controlled by Sheikh Hasina's Awami League after an election victory last June, repealed an ordinance protecting the alleged killers from prosecution.
The ordinance was passed by Mujib's successor, President Khandaker Mushtaque Ahmed, and upheld by the following strongman head of state, General Ziaur Rahman, who was gunned down in 1981.
General Zia's widow, Begum Khaleda Zia, heads the Bangladesh Nationalist Party that lost to the Awami League in the June elections. She is Sheikh Hasina's arch-rival.
Six of the alleged masterminds of the coup against Mujib were given diplomatic posts overseas by Ahmed and General Zia, and have now absconded.
"The repeal of the indemnity ordinance has given the country's legal system a civilised structure," said Dr Arefin Siddiqui, former general-secretary of the Dhaka University Teachers' Association.
"People will now have a chance to know the truth about the 1975 killings. It's their right.
"The trial will act as a warning to those (in the army) who try to take power through killing and bypassing legal procedures."
Retired Major Hafizuddin, a member of parliament from the opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), said: "No political killing should go unpunished."
Commented parliamentarian Nur Kutub Alam Chowdhury of the Jatiya Party: "The trial should have been held long before. People have been kept in the dark deliberately. But it's better late than never,"
"Sheikh Hasina has taken a very bold and timely step by ordering the trial," said businessman Shahidul Islam. "We had been governed by the rule of the jungle for the past 21 years."
Independent analyst Motiur Rahman Chowdhury, editor of Banglabazar Patrika newspaper, said he supported the trial of Mujib's alleged assassins.
But he cautioned that the trial could expose the truth about past events that might "not only shake the country's political stability but also cause personal embarrassment for Hasina".
He cited figures who were prominent in 1975 who were now members of the ruling Awami league.
"Their exact role in 1975 will come under question during the trial and may reveal unpleasant truths," Chowdhury said.

Kazi Shamsur Rahman, a leader of the fundamentalist Jamaat-e-Islami party that opposed Bangladesh's 1971 independence from Pakistan, said: "The trial of the (alleged) Mujib killers will open a floodgate for other trials. Hasina will surely come under pressure for that."
Added Motiur Rahman Chowdhury: "The list of political killings in Bangladesh is endless. If all of them have to be put on trial the government will have hardly anything else to think of."
